p.src: Now the three of them passed through the woods and went inside, where they saw the fool trussed up in a tree, crying out incessantly in unbearable pain. The Pilgrim stepped forward and laughed. “Well, my fine son-in-law! Why haven’t you risen by this hour to thank your new family, or gone to Master to announce the happy news? Are you still here showing off your acrobatics? Hey! Where is your mother-in-law? Where is your wife? What a fine son-in-law you make, bound tight and hung up for torture!” When the fool heard him come to taunt and shame him, he clenched his teeth, endured the pain, and dared not cry out. Seeing this, Sha Monk could hardly bear it. He put down the luggage, stepped forward, untied the ropes, and rescued him. The fool merely kowtowed repeatedly to them, for in truth he was overwhelmed with shame. A lyric to the tune “The Moon over the West River” bears witness:

p.src: Bajie gathered earth into an altar, burned incense, and bowed toward the sky. The Pilgrim asked, “Did you recognize those bodhisattvas?” Bajie replied, “By then I had fainted and lost my senses, and everything swam before my eyes. How could I have recognized any of them?” The Pilgrim handed the note to Bajie. When Bajie saw that it was a verse, he grew still more ashamed. Sha Monk laughed. “Second Brother has quite a gift—you moved four bodhisattvas to come and arrange a marriage for you!” Bajie said, “Brother, speak of it no more. I have behaved disgracefully. From now on, I shall never again dare to act recklessly. Even if the burden breaks every bone in my body, I shall put my shoulder to the carrying-pole and follow Master to the Western Regions.” Tripitaka said, “Only if you mean what you say.”

p.src: The Pilgrim then led his master back onto the main road. After they had traveled for a long while, they suddenly saw a lofty mountain blocking their way. Tripitaka reined in his horse and stayed his whip, saying, “Disciples, there is a mountain ahead. We must be cautious, lest demons make mischief and harm our company.” The Pilgrim replied, “With the three of us before your horse, what demon need you fear?” Thus reassured, the elder continued onward. And that mountain was truly a fine one:

p.src: Tripitaka rejoiced upon his horse and said, “Disciple, throughout my journey west I have crossed many mountains and rivers, but all were rugged and perilously steep. None possessed scenery like this mountain; its secluded charm is truly extraordinary. If we are drawing near to Vulture Peak and have not far to go, we should compose ourselves and assume a solemn bearing before meeting the World-Honored One.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Far too soon! Far too soon! We are nowhere near arriving.” Sha Monk asked, “Elder Brother, how far are we from Vulture Peak?” The Pilgrim replied, “The whole journey is one hundred and eight thousand li, and we have not yet covered even one part in ten.” Bajie asked, “Brother, how many years will it take us to get there?” The Pilgrim answered, “As for this distance, you two worthy brothers could cover it in a dozen days or so; as for me, I could make fifty round trips in a single day and still have daylight to spare; but as for Master—forget it, forget it!” The Tang Monk asked, “Wukong, then when do you say we shall arrive?” The Pilgrim replied, “You could walk from childhood to old age, grow young again after becoming old, and repeat the cycle of age and youth a thousand times, yet it would still be difficult; yet if only you perceive your true nature and keep a sincere resolve, then wherever each thought turns back upon itself—that is the Sacred Mountain.” Sha Monk said, “Elder Brother, though this place is not Vulture Peak, judging by the scenery, some worthy person must surely dwell here.” The Pilgrim replied, “That is well said. There can be no evil spirits here. This must surely be the abode of holy monks or immortals. Let us enjoy the sights and proceed at our leisure.” But enough of that.

p.src: Now this mountain was called Longevity Mountain. On it stood a Daoist temple called the Five Villages Abbey. Within the abbey dwelt an immortal whose Daoist name was Zhenyuanzi and whose sobriquet was “Lord Equal to the World.” The abbey produced a wondrous treasure: a spiritual root formed when chaos first divided and primeval vastness was first distinguished, before heaven and earth had yet opened. Of all the Four Great Continents beneath heaven, only the Five Villages Abbey in the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift possessed it. It was called the Cinnabar of Returning Grass, and also the Ginseng Fruit. It blossomed once every three thousand years, bore fruit three thousand years later, and took another three thousand years to ripen; in round numbers, one had to wait ten thousand years before it could be eaten. Even in those ten thousand years, it produced only thirty fruits. Each fruit resembled an infant not yet three days old, complete with all four limbs and every facial feature. If one fortunate enough merely smelled the fruit, one would live for three hundred and sixty years; if one ate a single fruit, one would live for forty-seven thousand years.

p.src: That day, the Great Immortal Zhenyuan received an invitation from the Primordial Celestial Worthy to attend the Miro Palace in the Heaven of Highest Purity and hear a lecture on “The Dao-Fruit of the Primordial Unity.” Countless unfettered immortals had emerged from the Great Immortal’s school, and even now he had forty-eight disciples, all Perfected Ones who had attained the Way. That day he took forty-six of them to the upper realm to hear the lecture, leaving the two youngest to guard the abbey: one was called Qingfeng, Clear Breeze, and the other Mingyue, Bright Moon. Qingfeng was only one thousand three hundred and twenty years old, while Mingyue had just turned one thousand two hundred. Zhenyuanzi instructed the two lads, “I cannot disobey the Great Celestial Worthy’s invitation and must go to Miro Palace for the lecture. You two must take good care of things at home. Before long, an old acquaintance of mine will pass this way. Be sure not to treat him discourteously. Pick two of my Ginseng Fruits for him to eat, as a token of our friendship in former days.” The two lads asked, “Who is this old acquaintance of Master’s? Please tell your disciples, so that we may receive him properly.” The Great Immortal replied, “He is a holy monk under the sovereign of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land. His religious name is Tripitaka, and he is now journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures.” The two lads laughed. “Confucius said, ‘Those who follow different Ways do not take counsel together.’ We belong to the mystic school of the Great Unity. How could we have any acquaintance with that Buddhist monk?” The Great Immortal said, “You know nothing of the matter. That monk is the reincarnation of the Golden Cicada, the second disciple of the sacred elder of the West, the Tathagata Buddha. Five hundred years ago, I met him at the Ullambana Assembly. He personally served me tea, honoring me as a disciple of the Buddha; for that reason he is an old acquaintance of mine.”

p.src: Tripitaka dismounted from the saddle and saw, to the left of the mountain gate, a stone tablet inscribed with ten large characters: “Mount Longevity, a blessed land; Five Villages Abbey, a celestial retreat.” The elder said, “Disciples, this truly is a Taoist abbey.” Friar Sand said, “Master, judging by this fresh and splendid scenery, good people must dwell within. Let us go in and look. When our journey is fulfilled and we return east, this too will be a sight worth remembering.” The Pilgrim said, “Well said.” So they all went in together and saw a pair of spring couplets on the second gate: “A mansion of immortals, forever young and deathless; A household of Taoists, as long-lived as Heaven.” The Pilgrim laughed. “This Taoist boasts outrageously to frighten people. Five hundred years ago, when old Monkey raised havoc in Heaven, I never saw such words even at the gate of the Most High Lord Lao.” Pigsy said, “Never mind that. Let us go in. Perhaps this Taoist really does possess some virtue; who can say?”

p.src: The boys drew back their shoulders, bowed low, and came forward to welcome them, saying, “Venerable master, forgive us for failing to meet you. Please be seated.” Delighted, the elder followed the two boys into the main hall to look around. It proved to be a five-bay hall facing south, fitted throughout with carved latticework, bright above and dark below. The immortal youths pushed open the lattice doors and invited the Tang monk inside. In the center of the wall he saw the two great characters “Heaven and Earth,” fashioned in many colors. Before them stood a vermilion, carved-lacquer incense table bearing a golden censer and vase, with sticks of incense neatly laid beside the censer.

p.src: The Tang monk stepped forward, pinched up incense with his left hand, placed it in the censer, and bowed three times in a full circuit of worship. When he had finished, he turned and said, “Immortal youths, your Five Villages Abbey is truly a realm of immortals in the West. Why do you not enshrine the Three Pure Ones, the Four Emperors, and all the celestial rulers, but offer incense only to the two words ‘Heaven and Earth’?” The boy laughed. “To tell you the truth, venerable master, of those two words, the one above rightly deserves our reverence; but the one below is not yet worthy to receive our incense. Our master included it merely out of flattery.” Tripitaka asked, “What do you mean by flattery?” The boy replied, “The Three Pure Ones are our master’s friends, and the Four Emperors are his old acquaintances; the Nine Luminaries are his juniors, and the Gods of the Years are his lesser guests.” At these words, the Pilgrim laughed until he toppled over. Pigsy asked, “Brother, what are you laughing at?” The Pilgrim said, “People say only old Monkey knows how to play tricks, but it turns out this Taoist boy can tie up the wind itself with his boasting.” Tripitaka asked, “Where is your master?” The boy replied, “The Primordial Celestial Worthy sent our master an invitation to the Miro Palace in the Heaven of Supreme Purity to hear a discourse on the ‘Fruition of the Primordial Way.’ He is not at home.” Unable to contain himself, the Pilgrim shouted, “You shameless Taoist brat! You do not even know whom you are speaking to. Before whom are you playing these tricks and putting on such an empty show? Who in the Miro Palace is a Great Unity Celestial Immortal? What could they possibly invite that wretched ox-hoofed master of yours to lecture about?”

p.src: Seeing him grow angry, Tripitaka feared the boy would answer back and provoke a quarrel, so he said, “Wukong, cease contending. Since we have entered only to leave at once, we would appear discourteous. As the saying goes, ‘An egret does not eat the flesh of another egret.’ Since their master is away, why cause them trouble? Go tether the horse before the mountain gate. Let Friar Sand guard the luggage, and have Pigsy unpack some rice and grain. Borrow their pot and stove and cook us a meal; when we leave, give them a few coins for firewood, and that will settle it. Each of you attend to your task and let me rest here awhile. We shall leave as soon as we have eaten.” The three of them duly went off to perform their respective tasks.

p.src: Mingyue and Qingfeng secretly praised him without end: “What a fine monk! He truly is the beloved sage of the West descended to the mortal world, his original spirit undimmed. Master ordered us to receive the Tang monk and give him ginseng fruit to eat as a token of their old friendship; he also told us to beware of trouble from his followers. Sure enough, those three look fierce and unruly and have coarse dispositions. Fortunately, we have managed to send them all away; if they were beside him, how could we let him see the ginseng fruit?” Qingfeng said, “Brother, we still do not know whether that monk truly is Master’s old acquaintance. Let us ask him, lest we make a mistake.” The two boys stepped forward again and asked, “May we inquire whether the venerable master is Tang Tripitaka, traveling from the Great Tang to the Western Heaven in search of scriptures?” Returning their courtesy, the elder said, “I am indeed. How did you immortal youths come to know my humble name?” The boy replied, “Before departing, our master instructed his disciples to go far out to welcome you. We did not expect your honored arrival so soon and failed to greet you properly. Please be seated, venerable master, while your disciples prepare tea to offer you.” Tripitaka said, “You are too kind.” Mingyue hurried back to their room, fetched a cup of fragrant tea, and offered it to the elder. When the tea was finished, Qingfeng said, “Brother, we must not disobey Master’s command. Let us go and fetch the fruit.”

p.src: The two boys took leave of Tripitaka and went together to their room. One took the golden striker, the other the cinnabar tray, lining its bottom with an extra green silk cloth; then they went straight to the ginseng orchard. Qingfeng climbed the tree and used the golden striker to knock down the fruit. Mingyue waited beneath the tree to catch it with the cinnabar tray. Presently they knocked down two fruits and caught them in the tray. They went straight to the front hall and presented them, saying, “Master Tang, our Five Villages Abbey stands in a remote and barren mountain, and we have nothing worthy to offer. Here are two humble fruits of our soil to quench your thirst for the moment.” At the sight of them, the elder trembled and drew three feet away, crying, “Merciful Buddha! Merciful Buddha! The harvest has been plentiful this year, so why has this abbey fallen to devouring people in famine? These are infants not yet three days old. How could you offer them to quench my thirst?” Qingfeng thought to himself, “This monk has lived amid fields of wrangling tongues and seas of right and wrong until his eyes have become those of an ordinary fleshly mortal; he cannot recognize the wondrous treasure of our immortal house.” Mingyue stepped forward and said, “Venerable master, this is called ginseng fruit. There is no harm in eating one.” Tripitaka said, “Nonsense, nonsense! Who knows how much suffering their parents endured in pregnancy before giving birth to them? They are not yet three days old. How can you already bring them here as fruit?” Qingfeng said, “They truly grew on a tree.” The elder said, “Absurd, absurd! Can a tree bear human beings? Take them away! To do such a thing is inhuman.”

p.src: Beyond the vegetable garden he saw yet another gate. He pushed it open and looked. Ah! Right in the center stood a great tree, its green branches richly fragrant and its verdant leaves casting a deep shade. The leaves resembled those of the plantain. The tree rose over a thousand feet, and its trunk measured seven or eight fathoms around at the roots. The Pilgrim leaned against the tree and looked up. On a southward branch he saw a ginseng fruit peeping out, and it truly resembled a little child. A stem grew from its tail end, fastening it to the branch. Its hands and feet moved about, its head nodded and swayed, and when the wind passed it even seemed to make a sound. Overjoyed, the Pilgrim praised it to himself: “What a splendid thing! Rare indeed! Rare indeed!” Bracing himself against the trunk, he shot upward with a whoosh. After all, there was nothing that monkey did better than climbing trees and stealing fruit. He tapped it once with the golden striker, and the fruit dropped to the ground with a thud. He leaped down after it and searched, but it had vanished without a trace; he searched through the grass on every side, but found no sign of it anywhere.

p.src: “Strange, strange,” said the Pilgrim. Perhaps it has feet and can walk, but even if it ran, it could not have leaped over the wall. I know what happened. The local earth god of this garden must have forbidden old Monkey to steal the fruit and taken it away.” He formed a hand seal, uttered an “Om” spell, and summoned the garden’s local earth god, who came before the Pilgrim, bowed, and said, “Great Sage, for what command has Your Holiness summoned this humble god?” The Pilgrim said, “Do you not know that old Monkey is the most notorious chief of thieves under heaven? In former years I stole the peaches of immortality, pilfered the imperial wine, and purloined the divine elixir, yet no one ever dared claim a share from me. Why, when I steal just one of their fruits today, do you snatch away my rightful share? This fruit grows upon a tree, so even birds passing through the sky should have a share. What great harm could there be in old Monkey eating just one? Why did you scoop it away the instant I knocked it down?” The earth god replied, “The Great Sage has wrongly accused this humble god. This treasure belongs to the terrestrial immortals, while this humble god is merely a ghost immortal. How would I dare take it? I am not even blessed enough to smell its fragrance.”

p.src: Pilgrim said, “If you did not take it, how did it disappear the moment I knocked it down?” The local earth god replied, “Great Sage, you know only that this treasure prolongs life, but you do not know its nature and origin.” Pilgrim asked, “What is there to know about its origin?” The earth god said, “This treasure blossoms once every three thousand years, bears fruit after another three thousand, and takes a further three thousand years to ripen. In nearly ten thousand years, it bears only thirty fruits. One fortunate enough merely to smell one will live for three hundred and sixty years; and one who eats a fruit will live for forty-seven thousand years. Yet it is incompatible with each of the Five Elements.” Pilgrim asked, “How is it incompatible with the Five Elements?” The earth god replied, “The fruit falls when it meets metal, withers when it meets wood, dissolves when it meets water, scorches when it meets fire, and sinks away when it meets earth. It must be struck with a metal implement before it will fall. Once it has been knocked down, it must be caught on a tray padded with a silk handkerchief. If it so much as touches a wooden vessel, it withers, and eating it will no longer prolong one’s life. To eat it, one must place it in porcelain, dissolve it in clear water, and then consume it. If it meets fire, it is scorched and rendered useless. As for sinking into earth, Great Sage, when you knocked that fruit to the ground just now, it burrowed straight into the soil. This soil is forty-seven thousand years old; even a steel drill could not bore into it in the slightest. It is several degrees harder than pig iron, and that is why anyone who eats the fruit gains longevity. If you do not believe me, Great Sage, try striking the ground and see.” Pilgrim at once drew out his gold-banded cudgel and thrust it down. With a ringing crash the cudgel sprang back, leaving not the slightest mark upon the ground. Pilgrim said, “It is true indeed, true indeed. My cudgel smashes stone to powder and leaves a mark even on pig iron. How is it that this blow could not damage the ground in the least? If that is so, I have falsely accused you. You may go back.” The earth god thereupon returned to his own shrine.

p.src: The Great Sage then devised a plan. He climbed the tree, wielded the golden striker with one hand, and with the other lifted the skirt of his brocade robe to form a pouch beneath the fruit. Parting branches and leaves, he knocked down three fruits and caught them in the fold of his robe. He leapt down from the tree and went straight back to the kitchen. Bajie smiled and asked, “Brother, did you get them?” Pilgrim replied, “Are these not what you wanted? Once Old Sun puts his hand to something, it is as good as caught. But we must not eat these fruits behind Sha Monk’s back. Call him over.” Bajie beckoned and called, “Wujing, come here.” Sha Monk set down the luggage, hurried into the kitchen, and asked, “Brothers, what did you call me for?” Pilgrim opened the fold of his robe and asked, “Brother, what do you think these are?” When Sha Monk saw them, he said, “They are ginseng fruits.” Pilgrim exclaimed, “Well now! So you recognize them. Where have you eaten them before?” Sha Monk replied, “Though I have never eaten one, in former days, when I served as the Curtain-Raising General and attended the imperial carriage at the Peach Banquet, I saw immortals from beyond the seas present these fruits to the Queen Mother in celebration of her birthday. I have seen them, certainly, but never tasted one. Brother, might you give me a little to taste?” Pilgrim said, “There is no need to ask. We brothers shall have one apiece.”

p.src: The three of them each enjoyed one of the three fruits. Bajie had a great appetite and a large mouth. He had begun to feel ravenously hungry as soon as he heard the young attendants eating, and now, the moment he saw the fruit, he seized it, opened his mouth wide, and swallowed it whole with a gulp. Then, rolling his eyes and feigning ignorance, he asked Pilgrim and Sha Monk, “What is it that you two are eating?” Sha Monk replied, “Ginseng fruit.” Bajie asked, “What does it taste like?” Pilgrim said, “Wujing, pay him no heed. You ate yours before either of us, and now you ask us?” Bajie said, “Brother, I ate mine too hastily. I did not chew slowly as you did and savor its taste. I did not even find out whether it had a pit before I swallowed it. Brother, when you do a kindness, see it through to the end. Now that you have roused my appetite, go and fetch another so Old Pig can eat it slowly.” Pilgrim replied, “Brother, you truly do not know when enough is enough. This is not like rice or flour food, of which one may eat one’s fill whenever one comes upon it. Only thirty such fruits grow in ten thousand years. For us to eat even one apiece is an extraordinary stroke of fortune, no trifling matter. Enough, enough! What we had was plenty.” He rose slightly, slipped the golden striker through the window opening into the attendants’ room, and ignored Bajie completely.

p.src: The two hurried off and found the flower-garden gate standing open. Qingfeng said, “I closed this gate. How did it come to be open?” They hurried through the flower garden and found that the vegetable-garden gate was open as well. They rushed into the ginseng-fruit garden, stood beneath the tree, and repeatedly counted the fruits overhead. Whichever way they counted, there were only twenty-two. Mingyue asked, “Do you know how to reckon accounts?” Qingfeng replied, “I do. Tell me the figures.” Mingyue said, “There were originally thirty fruits. When Master opened the garden, two were shared and eaten, leaving twenty-eight; just now we knocked down two for the Tang Monk to eat, leaving twenty-six; but now only twenty-two remain. Does that not mean four are missing? There is no need to say more. That band of villains must have stolen them. Let us go and berate the Tang Monk.”

p.src: The two boys left the garden gate and went straight to the main hall, where they pointed at the Tang Monk and poured out an unbroken stream of filthy abuse, mocking him from his bald crown to his bare nape; They called him a sneaking, rat-faced thief and shouted every foul insult they could muster. Unable to bear it any longer, the Tang Monk said, “Immortal lads, what is all this commotion about? Calm yourselves. If you have something to say, speak slowly; there is no need to rave and ramble so.” Qingfeng said, “Are you deaf? Am I speaking some barbarian tongue that you cannot understand? You stole and ate our ginseng fruit—why should I not say so?” The Tang Monk asked, “What does a ginseng fruit look like?” Mingyue replied, “The thing we brought you to eat just now—the one you said looked like a child. What else could it be?” The Tang Monk said, “Amitabha! The very sight of that thing made my heart quake with terror. How could I possibly dare steal and eat it? Even if I were dying of gluttony, I would never dare commit such thievery. Do not accuse an innocent man.” Qingfeng said, “You may not have eaten them, but one of your disciples may well have stolen them.” Sanzang said, “That is possible. Stop shouting for the moment and let me question them. If they truly stole the fruit, I shall make them compensate you.” Mingyue cried, “Compensate us! Even if you had the money, where could you buy such fruit?” Sanzang replied, “Even if money cannot buy it anywhere, the proverb says, ‘Honor and righteousness are worth a thousand pieces of gold.’ I shall make him apologize to you, and that will settle the matter. Besides, we do not yet know whether it was truly one of them.” Mingyue said, “How could it not be them? They divided the fruit unevenly and are still squabbling about it over there.” Sanzang called out, “Disciples, come here—all of you.” When Friar Sand heard him, he said, “This is bad. The secret is out. Master is calling us, and the little Daoist boys are hurling abuse. If word of what happened has not leaked out, what else could it be?” The Pilgrim said, “What a mortal shame! It was only a bit of food, but if the truth comes out, everyone will know us for thieves and gluttons. Just deny it.” Bajie said, “Exactly, exactly. Let us brazen it out.” The three of them had no choice but to leave the kitchen and go up to the main hall.

They divided the fruit unevenly and are still squabbling about it over there.”
Sanzang called out, “Disciples, come here—all of you.”
When Friar Sand heard him, he said, “This is bad. The secret is out.
Master is calling us, and the little Daoist boys are hurling abuse. If word of what happened has not leaked out, what else could it be?”
The Pilgrim said, “What a mortal shame!
It was only a bit of food, but if the truth comes out, everyone will know us for thieves and gluttons. Just deny it.”
Bajie said, “Exactly, exactly. Let us brazen it out.”
The three of them had no choice but to leave the kitchen and go up to the main hall.
